metadata.title: Their Numbers, My Arrows - Reading an AI Announcement Without Adding to It
metadata.subject_line: Separating what a company said from what you added
metadata.playlist: Agentic AI Adoption in Financial Services
notes: STRUCTURE: two-column ledger, audited line by line. NOT a numbered framework - v1 used four questions and was scrapped for being the same FORM as bs-01-pick-and-scope. Compare form against the previous film, not argument.
VOICE af_bella, chosen by ear from an A/B against am_onyx. Bella measures 3.21 w/s against Onyx's 3.76 - about 70s longer across the film. Also the toolkit's documented hai persona default.

TONE POLICY: HSBC is the good example, not the target. All three outlets (Kingy AI, Metaintro, InfotechLead) reported correctly and are shown as correct. The only person who got anything wrong in this film is the narrator.

Q3's evidence is PRIMARY: two different $1.5bn figures inside HSBC's own FY2025 transcript. The earlier plan to name outlets for an error was dropped - verification showed they made none. See VERIFICATION.md.
Every figure self-reported and unaudited (case study 6.7). Stated once, plainly, at B03.
B10 is relabelled, not struck - the agentic reading survives as a revisable inference with its overturn condition on screen.
GRAPHIC beats are Manim, provided by scenes.py. run.sh detects `class <BID>_<Name>(Scene)` by regex over raw text - never use a base class, and never write that pattern literally in a comment.

B03 TRIMMED after measuring audio: it ran 62.9s, the longest beat, because it recited five figures the ledger already displays with their sources. The narration now points at the screen instead ('they're on screen with their sources; I'm not going to recite them at you') and keeps only what the visual cannot carry: the two $1.5bn lines flagged because B07 pays them off, the self-reported/unaudited caveat, and HSBC's assistive-not-autonomous wording. Same redundancy PROOF flagged on Film 5's B03.

V1 (PROOF interim #2): B05 asserted absence across three named documents. The case study's own wording is narrower — HSBC has not stated the connection 'in any disclosure this case study identified'. Scoped to the check actually performed ('I couldn't find...'). A film about not claiming more than the source supports cannot enumerate documents it did not exhaustively audit.

S1 (PROOF interim #2): B07's gate contract required both $1.5bn quotes in frame; the ledger showed paraphrases plus the source. The narration reads two verbatim sentences, and PLAYBOOK 1b records unshown quotes as the most repeated failure across these films. B07 now uses a dedicated scene carrying both verbatim quotes with the transcript named and dated.

beats.narration_text: Hi, this is Tanmay Kulkarni from Humanitarians AI.

Here's a paragraph I wrote about HSBC, before I checked anything. "HSBC's engineers got dramatically faster using AI. The bank switched off more than a thousand old systems, found one point two billion dollars in savings, and is moving another one and a half billion into growth. AI is making this bank leaner." Every number in that paragraph is real. Every number came from HSBC. And the last sentence — the one that ties it together, the one that makes it a story — I made that up. Not deliberately. I just… wrote it. Because that's what those numbers look like when you put them next to each other.

props.segment: A paragraph I wrote before I checked anything
props.command: "AI is making this bank leaner."  <- I made that sentence up.

beats.narration_text: So I did something simple, and it's the only method in this video. Two columns. On the left, everything HSBC actually said. On the right, everything I added. Then I go through the right-hand column, line by line, and try to move each one across to the left. Whatever won't move, I made up.

shot.description: Two-column ledger, empty. WHAT HSBC ACTUALLY SAID | WHAT I ADDED.

beats.narration_text: Left column first. Everything on it is HSBC's own figure, from HSBC's own results and transcripts — the speed-ups, the applications retired, the savings realised. They're on screen with their sources; I'm not going to recite them at you. Two of them I do need you to notice, though, because they come back. One and a half billion in simplification saves, going straight to the bottom line. And one and a half billion in reallocation costs, going into growth. All of these are self-reported and unaudited, with no published methodology behind them. That isn't a complaint — it's just what they are, and you should know it. And notice the care in HSBC's language. Coding assistants, that engineers use. Assistive. They never once call them autonomous.

shot.description: Left column fills: five sourced, dated HSBC disclosures.

beats.narration_text: Now the right column. And this is the uncomfortable part, because I have to write down what I actually thought. AI made them faster, so the bank needed fewer people. The numbers imply a method I could go and inspect. One and a half billion means one thing. Somebody out there has definitely got this wrong. And their coding tools are not agentic AI. Five lines. I believed all five of them. Not one of them came from HSBC.

shot.description: Right column fills: five things the narrator added.

beats.narration_text: First line. AI made them faster, so the bank needed fewer people, so it saved money. Go and look for that in the filings. It isn't there. I couldn't find HSBC connecting the coding assistants to the headcount savings anywhere — not in the transcript, not in the investor presentation, not in the release. They don't deny it either. They simply never join those two things up. So that line doesn't move. That line was mine.

Second line. The numbers imply a method. Sixty percent faster, five times faster — surely somebody measured something, and I can go and read how they did it. Faster than what? Measured how? Which tool, which model, against which baseline? None of it is disclosed. Anywhere. The most technical thing on the entire public record is HSBC's chief executive calling them — and I do genuinely love this — "vibe coding assistants." The outcome is real. The method is absent. And I had quietly assumed one from the other.
beats.tone: attentive, and genuinely amused at the quote.

beats.narration_text: Third line. And this is where I stopped and read it twice. One and a half billion means one thing. Except in that one transcript — one document, one morning in February — HSBC uses one and a half billion dollars twice. Here's the first. "We are taking one point five billion dollars of annualised simplification saves straight to the bottom line." That's money they're keeping. And here's the second, further down the same call. "We are also making positive progress with the reallocation of circa one point five billion dollars from non-strategic or low-returning businesses." That's money they're moving. Same figure. Opposite jobs. And nobody hid anything. Both sentences are sitting right there, in HSBC's own words, minutes apart. But if you'd skimmed that call and walked away holding one number — there's a decent chance you'd be holding the wrong one.

shot.description: Both verbatim $1.5bn sentences in frame together, transcript named and dated. Scene: B07_QuotePair.

beats.narration_text: And it isn't a one-off. One point eight billion dollars. In February twenty twenty-five, that figure meant severance and restructuring costs. In February twenty twenty-six, the same figure means reallocation — one and a half billion of it, plus three hundred million in Hang Seng cost synergies, recycled back into growth. Same number. Different year. A completely different meaning.

shot.description: $1.8bn: FY2024 severance beside FY2025 reallocation, each dated.

beats.act: strike four · there was no culprit
beats.narration_text: Fourth line. Somebody out there must have got this wrong. This is the one I'm least proud of. Because my instinct wasn't to go and check my own reading — it was to go and find somebody else's mistake. Some outlet that had grabbed one point eight billion and called it an AI investment. I found three publications that covered it. All three of them got it right. Kingy AI spelled out that it was a reallocation, not new money. Metaintro gave the same breakdown. InfotechLead put the word "reallocates" in the headline. There was no culprit. So I stopped looking for one, and went and read HSBC's transcript myself — which is where the good example had been sitting the whole time. That line doesn't move either. And it's the one that taught me the most. The danger here isn't that people are careless. It's that a number can honestly mean two things, and you still have to go and check.

props.artifactTitle: I went looking for a mistake
artifactLines: Kingy AI - "isn't spending new money on this transformation"
The better example was in HSBC's own transcript.
props.sparkLine: Secondary first, primary second. That was the wrong order.

beats.narration_text: Fifth line. Their coding tools are not agentic AI. And this one I'm not striking out. I'm relabelling it. Because HSBC does use the word agentic. In June, four months after those productivity figures, they announced a financial-crime system with Google Cloud — and there, they used it. Agentic. Their word, not mine. So one system gets called agentic and the other one doesn't. That's real, and I think it means something. But HSBC has never said "our coding assistants are not agentic AI." Nobody at HSBC put those two announcements next to each other. I did. So this line stays on the right, greyed out, with a label on it. My reading. Revisable. If HSBC describes those coding tools in agentic terms next quarter, I'm not going to defend this. I'd just be wrong, and I'd change it.

shot.description: Fifth entry greyed and tagged, WITH the revision condition on screen. Scene: B10_LedgerRelabelCondition.

beats.narration_text: There's one more place this happened, and it's the part I actually enjoyed. I built a small working version of that patching pipeline. Four stages: a vulnerability comes in, the assistant drafts a fix, a human reviews it, then it gets applied and tested. And at the review stage, I had to decide what the criteria were. Auto-approve anything below a certain severity? Require a sign-off above some confidence score? I couldn't do it. Because HSBC has never described a code review gate. They've stated a general principle — AI deployments get reviewed, monitored, audited — and that is the entire public record. So the gate in my version ships with no criteria at all. None. It refuses to run until somebody hands it one. It raises an error and stops. That empty gate is this whole video, written in code. If I'd invented a threshold there, I'd have implied HSBC works in a way nobody has said they work.

shot.description: Pipeline: Intake -> Assistant -> Review Gate (empty) -> Apply & Test.

beats.narration_text: So where does that leave you? Because both of the easy answers are wrong. You can't assume the connection — nobody stated it. But you can't assume there isn't one either. HSBC hasn't denied it, and it would be a perfectly reasonable thing for faster engineering to feed into headcount decisions. It just isn't on the record. So what are you actually allowed to walk away with?

props.greeting: So what are you allowed to keep?
props.command: Assume the connection - nobody stated it. Assume there isn't one - nobody denied it.

beats.narration_text: This. The left column, on its own. HSBC's engineers got measurably faster at two specific tasks, by HSBC's own measurement. HSBC switched off one thousand, one hundred and sixty-five old applications. HSBC realised one point two billion dollars in simplification savings. And HSBC is moving one and a half billion of costs into growth — which is a different one and a half billion from the one going to the bottom line. Four things. All sourced. All dated. Not one of them explaining any of the others. That's smaller than the paragraph I opened with. It's also the version I could defend in a room full of people who'd read the filings. And that trade — a smaller thing you can actually hold, instead of a bigger thing you can't — that's the whole point of the two columns.

shot.description: The left column alone. Right column gone.

beats.narration_text: Your turn, and it's one instruction. Take any AI announcement — a press release, an earnings call, a vendor page. Make two columns. On the left, only what they actually said. On the right, everything you added. Then try to move each right-hand line across. You've done it right if your right column barely empties. That isn't failure — that's you finding out how much of the reading was yours. You've done it wrong if everything slides across on the first try. That means you're filling the left column in your own handwriting.

props.command: Make two columns. Left: only what they said. Right: everything you added. Move each line left.
props.runningText: good: your right column barely empties

beats.narration_text: Their numbers. My arrows. It's worth knowing which is which. This is Tanmay Kulkarni, from Humanitarians AI.
